\chapter{Synthesis --- What You Understand, and What You Don't}
\label{ch:spanish-synthesis-verbs-of-mind}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report which part of what I heard landed and which did not, instead of only signalling that I am lost.}

The chapter-14 distress signal becomes a sentence with moving parts.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — what you understand, and what you don't}

\label{lesson:ES-C34-sintesis-mente}



\begin{quote}
Say the sentence you learned in the repair kit, the one that rescues a conversation. (\emph{No entiendo.})
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the formula was a verb all along}]
You have been saying \textbf{no entiendo} since the repair kit, and until four chapters ago it was a single frozen block — two sounds that meant \emph{I'm lost}, with no moving parts.

It has parts now. \textbf{Entiendo} is \emph{entender}, and \emph{entender} is Latin \emph{intendere}, \textquotedblleft{}to stretch toward.\textquotedblright{} Which means the sentence you have been using to admit defeat has never actually said \emph{I failed}. It says:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{I am not managing to stretch that far.}
\end{quote}

That was true the whole time. You just could not see it yet.

And the moment a formula has parts, it turns. \emph{No entiendo} stops being the only thing you can say and becomes one option among several.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Back in the repair kit, all you could do:

\begin{quote}
— No entiendo. Más despacio, por favor.
\end{quote}

Now, the same moment, with the parts working:

\begin{quote}
— Perdón — \textbf{leo} un poco, pero \textbf{no entiendo}. — Más despacio, por favor. \textbf{Ahora entiendo.} Gracias.
\end{quote}

Same trouble. But the second speaker is no longer only failing — they are reporting \textbf{which} part works and which does not. That is the difference between a distress signal and a conversation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four verbs is not four words. It is the ability to say \textbf{where} you are in a language: what you take in, what you work on, what lands, what you can produce.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the repair-kit version — the distress signal on its own
  \item the version above, where you say what \emph{does} work before what doesn't
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run the second one until it sounds like a person, not a repair kit.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb was hiding inside \emph{no entiendo}? (\emph{Entender}.) What did it physically mean? (\textbf{To stretch toward}.) What can you say now that you could not say back then? (Not just that you are lost — \textbf{which part} is lost.)
\end{tcolorbox}
